samples.summary: The per-account device secret outlives the session it protects: nothing removes it on session expiry or tab close, and no sweep reaches localStorage
samples.evidence:
`forgetDeviceSecret` has exactly one production caller — `eraseOfflineData` (offline-erase.ts:39) — which runs only from (a) a deliberate logout whose server request returned ok, (b) `retryPendingOfflineErase` for ids recorded by a *failed deliberate* erase, and (c) the preference being switched off. None of those fire when a session simply expires (auth.ts:277 sets `eraseLocalData: "none"` on the 401 arm) or when the browser is closed. `WafflebaseDocStore.collectStale` sweeps IndexedDB headers, archives and orphan snapshots — it never touches localStorage — so the design's stated bound (offline-local-persistence.md:396, "the residual ... is bounded by the thirty-day sweep and by that erase's own retry") does not hold for the secret at all: `wafflebase-durable-device:{userId}` persists indefinitely.

Vector: user A uses the feature on a shared machine and their session expires (or they close the tab). User B signs in on the same browser profile. localStorage is partitioned per *origin*, not per account, so B's page can enumerate `localStorage` for keys prefixed `wafflebase-durable-device:` and read A's secret directly — the per-account split at durable-session.ts:128 does not remove the shared ingredient it claims to (offline-local-persistence.md:392). With A's secret, B reconstructs `wb:{secret}:{A.userId}:{docKey}` for any document id they know (both remaining ingredients are public to a workspace peer, as the file's own comment at line 84 states). Confirmed against the backend: `packages/backend/src/document/yorkie-auth.controller.ts:69` puts `ActivateClient`/`DeactivateClient` in `CLIENT_METHODS`, and line 245-247 states "Client-scoped methods carry no document; a valid token is enough" — so B, holding their own perfectly valid Yorkie token, can deactivate A's per-document durable client, or activate under the same key and reproduce the one-actor/two-writers state the module itself describes as silent edit loss (lines 13-18). Once read, the capability is retained off the device indefinitely, which is a strict escalation over the local disk read B already had.

Fix direction: mint the secret in `sessionStorage`, or sweep `wafflebase-durable-device:*` entries whose account has no remaining store rows during `collectStale`, or drop it whenever `fetchMeOptional` resolves `null` for the account that owns it.

samples.summary: Offline document content survives an expired session on a shared device for up to thirty days, and two of the three mitigations the design names cannot reach it
samples.evidence:
`eraseLocalData: "none"` on the `fetchWithAuth` 401 arm means a session that expires erases nothing, and a closed tab erases nothing either. The design defends this (offline-local-persistence.md:224) by naming three covers: "that sign-out, ... the 30-day sweep, and the reconcile the next session runs". Two of those cannot apply. The deliberate sign-out did not happen — that is the premise of the case. And the reconcile cannot reach it: `purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments` (offline-erase.ts:469-477) resolves `who = offlineUserId()` and builds `new WafflebaseDocStore({ userId: who })`, and every delete it performs goes through `purgeDocument`, whose candidate set is `headerKeysWhere(BY_USER, IDBKeyRange.only(this.userId))`. When user B signs in next, `who` is B, so the reconcile is structurally incapable of touching A's rows.

That leaves `collectStale` alone, which is age-based at thirty days. So on the shared workstation / lab machine / borrowed laptop the design names as the motivating threat (offline-local-persistence.md:~170), a previous user's full document content — snapshots and un-pushed change logs, gzip-compressed but not encrypted — remains readable in IndexedDB by anyone who opens devtools, or by any XSS on the origin, for up to thirty days after their session ends. Session expiry and tab-close are the commonest way a session ends on exactly such a machine.

I am reporting this because the stated mitigation is factually wrong rather than because the tradeoff (preserving un-pushed work) is indefensible; a cover that names three mechanisms of which only one applies makes the residual look a great deal smaller than it is. A cheap narrowing would be to erase only entries whose change log is empty on a 401 — those genuinely are copies of what the server holds — and keep the ones carrying unsent work.

samples.summary: The PDF branch of the share route returns before `NonDurableScope`, so share-link PDF comment documents are kept off a visitor's disk by the temporary `pdf-` prefix exclusion alone
samples.evidence:
`SharedDocumentInner` early-returns `<SharedPdfLayout .../>` at line 967-980, above the `<NonDurableScope>` added at line 1016. `SharedPdfLayout` (line 759) renders `PdfCollabProvider`, which renders `CollabDocumentProvider` with `docKey={`pdf-${documentId}`}` (app/files/pdf-collab.tsx:200). So on that branch `useDurabilityPermitted()` answers the default `true`, and the only thing refusing durability is `isExcluded(docKey)` in lib/use-durable-document.ts (`docKey.startsWith("pdf-")`).

Today that single guard holds, so this is not currently exploitable. It matters because the design states the PDF exclusion as explicitly temporary — "PDF is excluded until it has a chip" (offline-local-persistence.md:~150) — whereas the share-link exclusion is permanent and security-motivated. The day someone gives PDF a sync chip and lifts the prefix rule, this branch silently becomes durable for a signed-in visitor on somebody else's share link: their own `wb:…:{userId}:pdf-{id}` client, authenticating with `fetchYorkieToken` (their personal token) rather than the `fetchYorkieShareToken` whose role and expiry the auth webhook validates, writing the shared document's comment content to a disk the link's revocation cannot reach — which is precisely the vulnerability `NonDurableScope` was introduced to close for the other five types. Wrapping the whole of `SharedDocumentInner`'s return (or `SharedDocument` itself) rather than only the non-blob branch costs one line and removes the coupling.

samples.summary: The durability permission context is default-permit, so a future public or capability-scoped route is durable unless it remembers to opt out
samples.evidence:
`const DurabilityPermitted = createContext(true);` makes persistence permitted everywhere by default, and the refusal is expressed only by one `NonDurableScope` wrapper in `app/shared/shared-document.tsx:1016`. I enumerated every `CollabDocumentProvider` call site (document-detail.tsx:909, board-detail.tsx:260, notes-detail.tsx:377, slides-detail.tsx:951, docs-detail.tsx:350, files/pdf-collab.tsx:199, shared-document.tsx:1026-1089) and confirmed the gate is complete today: all but the share route are behind `PrivateRoute` in App.tsx:128.

The weakness is the default rather than a present bypass. This is an access-control decision — "may this subtree write document content to the visitor's disk?" — expressed as an opt-out, on a codebase that already gained one public capability-scoped document route and whose own comment (shared-document.tsx:1008) notes the exclusion cannot be derived from the document key. A second such route (an embed, a published view, a template preview that mounts an editor) is durable by default and nothing in the enforced path or the lint lanes would say so. Default-deny with an explicit `DurableScope` on the six private routes inverts the failure mode; failing that, an assertion that `permitted` is false whenever the Yorkie client was mounted with a share `authTokenInjector` would catch the class.

samples.summary: `randomSecret()` falls back to `Math.random()` for the client-key salt, which is the value's whole security property
samples.evidence:
`randomSecret()` uses `crypto.getRandomValues` when available and otherwise fills the 8 bytes with `Math.floor(Math.random() * 256)` (lines 143-145). `Math.random()` is not a CSPRNG in any engine — V8 uses xorshift128+ with a recoverable state — so a secret minted on that path is predictable from a handful of observed outputs, which defeats the sole purpose of the salt as documented at lines 80-94 (making `wb:{secret}:{userId}:{docKey}` underivable by a workspace peer who can then Activate/DeactivateClient against it, cf. backend yorkie-auth.controller.ts:245).

The inline comment claims the branch is unreachable because "`navigator.locks` and `crypto` are both secure-context APIs". `crypto.getRandomValues` is in fact available in insecure contexts (only `crypto.subtle` is secure-context-restricted), so the reasoning is wrong even though the practical reachability is near zero. Since the branch is effectively dead, the right fix is to delete it and throw (declining durability) rather than mint a guessable secret — the module already fails closed everywhere else for exactly this reason (lines 47-56).

samples.summary: The path-traversal regression guard was weakened from a per-request assertion to `some()`, so a raw id in a secondary request is no longer detected unless it happens to normalize onto `/auth/logout`
samples.evidence:
The suite previously asserted, for *every* request a call made, both `pathname).not.toContain("/auth/logout")` and `pathname).toContain(encodeURIComponent(TRAVERSAL))`. The change keeps the first per-URL (lines 162-164) but downgrades the second to `paths.some(...)` (lines 170-174), because `deleteWorkspace` now issues a companion `fetchDocuments()` carrying no id.

The reasoning for the relaxation is sound as far as it goes — a request that does not contain the id cannot smuggle it — and the `/auth/logout` check is the primary detector and still universal. The residual gap: a module that interpolates the id correctly in one request and *raw* in another now passes `some()`, and is only caught if that raw interpolation happens to normalize to the one fixture path the suite looks for. `TRAVERSAL = "../../auth/logout"` is tuned to two-level-up route shapes; a raw id at a different depth (`${BASE}/${id}` where BASE is one segment, or an id in a query string, which `new URL().pathname` drops entirely) would resolve somewhere else and both assertions would be silent. Since this file exists specifically to pin the `seg()` guard across every route-param call site (line 70-74), preserving the strength would be cheap: assert per-URL that each path either contains the encoded id or contains no trace of the raw one (`expect(raw).not.toContain(TRAVERSAL)` over every request, unencoded), rather than only asserting the fixture's particular landing spot.

verdict.reason: Verified independently. `wafflebase-durable-device:{userId}` is written in `deviceSecret()` (durable-session.ts:158-180) and removed only by `forgetDeviceSecret` (durable-session.ts:190-197), whose sole production caller is `eraseOfflineData` (offline-erase.ts:39). That function is reached only from a deliberate logout confirmed by the server (offline-erase.ts:332 via api/auth.ts:134 `eraseLocalData !== "none" && res?.ok`), from `retryPendingOfflineErase` for ids a failed deliberate erase recorded (offline-erase.ts:368), and from the preference-off watcher (offline-erase.ts:554). The 401/expiry arm explicitly passes `eraseLocalData: "none"` (api/auth.ts:277), so expiry clears nothing; there is no unload/pagehide handler and no `sessionStorage` usage anywhere in packages/frontend/src. `collectStale` (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1176-1244) sweeps only IndexedDB headers, archives and orphan snapshots — a repo-wide grep for `removeItem(` in the frontend shows no localStorage sweep of the secret prefix (the only prefix scan, durable-session.ts:200-218, is `resetDeviceSecretForTest`). So the bound asserted at durable-session.ts:119-123 and offline-local-persistence.md:394-396 does not hold. The downstream capability is real: yorkie-auth.controller.ts:69 and :245-248 allow `ActivateClient`/`DeactivateClient` on token validity alone, making the secret the only non-derivable ingredient of `wb:{secret}:{userId}:{docKey}` (durable-session.ts:84-94). In-lane as sensitive-secret retention beyond the session it protects; major, not critical, since the attacker needs prior access to the shared browser profile — the escalation is retaining the capability off-device indefinitely. No counterexample found after searching every localStorage/sessionStorage site, every reference to the secret, and every erase caller chain.

verdict.reason: Every element of the claim checks out against the code. auth.ts:255-281 passes `eraseLocalData: "none"` on the 401-after-failed-refresh arm, and logout's guard at auth.ts:134 (`eraseLocalData !== "none" && res?.ok`) therefore skips `eraseOfflineDataOnLogout()` entirely — nothing local is erased and the identity mirror is not even spent. The comment at auth.ts:271-273 (mirrored in the design at offline-local-persistence.md:197-198) names three covers, and two provably cannot apply to this case: the deliberate sign-out did not happen (premise), and the reconcile is user-scoped — purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments resolves `who = offlineUserId()` (offline-erase.ts:469) and builds a store for that user, while its enumeration (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:988-991) and every delete (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:917-920) use `headerKeysWhere(BY_USER, IDBKeyRange.only(this.userId))`. OfflineRuntime overwrites the remembered identity with the new signer at offline-runtime.tsx:66 before calling the reconcile at offline-runtime.tsx:157, so with user B signed in the reconcile cannot see, let alone delete, user A's rows. retryPendingOfflineErase (offline-erase.ts:360-380) is no help either: ids are only recorded when a *deliberate* erase fails (offline-erase.ts:343), never on the 401 path. That leaves only collectStale, the single cross-account sweep (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1176-1215), age-gated at DefaultMaxAgeMs = 30 days (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:218) and run once per session (offline-runtime.tsx:123). Net effect: on the shared-device threat model the design itself names (offline-local-persistence.md:156-158, 180-198), a departed user's full document snapshots and un-pushed change logs — gzip-compressed, not encrypted (offline-local-persistence.md:239-249) — remain readable in IndexedDB to anyone with devtools or any same-origin XSS for up to thirty days after their session expires or their tab closes. This is sensitive data exposure, squarely in the Security lane, and no guard elsewhere makes it unreachable. I could find no named ground (not-present / already-guarded / out-of-scope) on which to refute.

finding.summary: The `deviceSecret` salting the Yorkie client key is per-browser-profile, not per-account, so on the shared device this feature is designed for one signed-in user can derive every other user's per-document client key
finding.evidence:
`durableClientKey()` returns `wb:{deviceSecret}:{userId}:{docKey}` (durable-session.ts:96-98) and `deviceSecret()` reads a single `localStorage` key `wafflebase-durable-device` (line 110, 137-154) that is **not scoped to an account** — every user who signs in on that browser profile reads and writes the same value.

The module's own comment (lines 80-94) states the threat: Yorkie authorizes `ActivateClient`/`DeactivateClient` on token validity alone, so anybody holding any valid token who can *derive* a client key can activate or tear it down. I confirmed that authorization model in this repo: `packages/backend/src/document/yorkie-auth.controller.ts:69` defines `CLIENT_METHODS = new Set(['ActivateClient','DeactivateClient'])` and line 292-296 returns `ALLOW` for them with no document and no client-key ownership check; `docs/design/yorkie-auth-webhook.md:82` says the same ("No document. Validate token only").

Vector: attacker A signs in once on a shared/kiosk/borrowed browser profile and reads `localStorage['wafflebase-durable-device']`. From then on, from any machine, A computes `wb:{stolenSecret}:{B_userId}:{sheet-<docId>}` for any workspace peer B — `B_userId` is the sequential id every member list carries and `docId` sits in the URL, both public to a peer, exactly as the comment notes. Holding only A's own valid Yorkie token, A calls `DeactivateClient` (or activates the key first) against B's per-document client, stranding or taking over the durable session B's unsent work depends on.

Second, weaker vector on the same root cause: the "secret" is transmitted to the Yorkie server as part of the client key on every activate and stored in the client row, so it is not confidential against anything that can read a client listing, an admin view, or a server log that echoes a client key — and one leaked key yields the secret for the whole device, hence every user and document on it.

verdict.reason: The finding's central factual premise is not present in the code. `DEVICE_SECRET_PREFIX = "wafflebase-durable-device"` (durable-session.ts:125) is a prefix, not the storage key: `deviceSecretKey(userId)` returns `wafflebase-durable-device:{userId}` (durable-session.ts:128-130), and `deviceSecret(userId)` reads/writes localStorage only under that per-account key (durable-session.ts:158-167), with the storage-refused fallback also keyed by userId (durable-session.ts:173-178). `durableClientKey` passes the userId into the salt (durable-session.ts:96-98). Grep over the repo finds no read or write of a bare unscoped `wafflebase-durable-device` key. Therefore attacker A, signing in on the shared profile, obtains only `wafflebase-durable-device:{A_userId}`, which is not an ingredient of B's key `wb:{B_secret}:{B_userId}:{docKey}` — the described derivation of any peer's client key fails. The module comment the reviewer cites as stating the threat actually states the mitigation ("Per account, not per browser profile... One secret per account removes the shared ingredient", durable-session.ts:110-117), and `forgetDeviceSecret(userId)` drops the per-account entry on the sign-out erase (durable-session.ts:190-196, offline-erase.ts:39). Tests assert per-account separation (durable-session.test.ts:116-117). The backend ActivateClient/DeactivateClient allow-on-token-validity behaviour may be real, but it is only exploitable given a derivable client key, which is the part that does not hold.
